title: Three members seek a rate rise as oil cuts Japan’s growth outlook
summary: The Bank of Japan kept the overnight call-rate guideline near 0.75% on April 28. Six members voted for the decision and three favored an immediate rise to 1.0%. The April outlook, released at the same minute, describes the problem facing both sides. The Bank marked down fiscal 2026 activity sharply while raising its inflation forecast. More expensive oil was both a transfer of purchasing power out of Japan and a cost that domestic firms could pass on. The timing of monetary tightening depends on which effect persists beyond the initial oil shock (statement, voting note, and April Outlook, sections I–III).

The revisions were unusually informative about the shock’s sign. The median fiscal 2026 real growth forecast fell from 1.0% in January to 0.5%. CPI excluding fresh food went from 1.9% to 2.8%, a 0.9 percentage point increase. CPI excluding fresh food and energy rose from 2.2% to 2.6%. Even this narrower basket includes goods and services whose production or distribution uses fuel. Its revision alone cannot establish that domestic demand was stronger. Fiscal 2027 median forecasts stood at 0.7% for growth and 2.3% for CPI excluding fresh food. By fiscal 2028 the corresponding inflation median returned to 2.0% (April Outlook, forecast appendix).

Those projections relied on a specific path for oil and trade. The Bank assumed Dubai crude would fall from around US$105 per barrel toward US$70–80 by the end of the projection, without large-scale supply-chain disruption. Under that path, weaker terms of trade compressed household real incomes and corporate profits in fiscal 2026. Government measures, accommodative financing and the starting level of profits helped sustain moderate growth, with some recovery as the oil drag eased. A prolonged interruption in supply could reduce production, weaken labour demand and interrupt the wage-price cycle. It could also raise the prices of more goods and services as firms passed costs through. These risks can emerge together, which is why the majority judged growth risks to the downside and price risks to the upside, especially in fiscal 2026 (April Outlook, summary, section III and footnote 2).

The dissenters reached the same proposed rate by different routes. Junko Nakagawa emphasized the prevailing level of accommodation and upside price risks despite uncertainty over the Middle East. Hajime Takata thought the inflation target was broadly achieved and second-round effects from abroad already tilted the balance upward. Naoki Tamura wanted policy closer to the neutral rate because the balance of price risks had shifted substantially. The decision gives no numerical estimate of the neutral rate. Treating 1.0% as Tamura’s estimate would conflate his proposed next step with his assessment of where further adjustments should lead (statement, voting note).

The majority still foresaw additional increases. It expected underlying inflation to become broadly consistent with 2% between the second half of fiscal 2026 and fiscal 2027. The Bank viewed real rates as very low and wanted to prevent inflation overshooting sufficiently to harm the economy later. The oil path and firms’ responses determined how much time the Board had. If energy merely raised the price level while squeezing real incomes, pre-emptive tightening could aggravate weak demand. If wage settlements, expectations and prices of domestically supplied services reset in response, waiting would leave more inflation to offset later. These are competing transmission mechanisms for the same initial price increase (April Outlook, sections III–IV).

The official release time was 12:04 Japan time for both the rate statement and the Bank’s View. A market move at that point could reflect the wider set of dissenters, the sharp revisions or the Bank’s updated account of upside price risks. The absence of an actual rate change does not identify the size of the news. Compare rates expected at subsequent meetings, the exchange rate and inflation compensation using quotes known before 12:04, and treat the later press conference separately. The full text of the outlook was scheduled for April 30, so it should enter a historical market study on its own release date (statement, release reference).

questions.question: Did the market bring forward tightening even as the growth forecast fell?
questions.detail: Compare the change in overnight-indexed swap rates for the next two meetings with longer forwards at the 12:04 release. Use pre-meeting forecasts or surveys to determine what investors already knew about oil and expected of the vote. Record simultaneous foreign-rate and oil moves before assigning the change to Japanese policy.

questions.question: Which industries absorbed higher oil costs and which passed them on?
questions.detail: Map energy intensity and import exposure against selling-price revisions, operating margins and output. Compare firms in similar industries with different capacity to raise prices. Declining margins and hiring would support the purchasing-power channel, while broad price increases accompanied by stronger wage expectations would point to greater persistence.

questions.question: How sensitive was the policy outlook to the assumed fall in Dubai crude?
questions.detail: Compare the release-date futures curve, subsequent oil prices in yen and the path toward US$70–80 in the outlook. Vary both oil and exchange-rate assumptions when estimating effects on consumer prices. Keep the physical-disruption scenario separate, since changes in the availability of inputs can reduce output beyond the effect of a higher import bill.
